root.note: Reconstructed, not recorded: nobody has found the Gothic word in a text. The medieval Latin forms raupa, ropa and rauba are recorded.

history: Think of your wardrobe as war loot. Ropa comes from a Germanic word, reconstructed as *raupa, for what was taken in raids: goods, and very often clothing. It came into medieval Latin as raupa, ropa and rauba, by now meaning cloth in general, from bedspreads to fine dresses. The violence hasn't quite gone. The related verb gave Spanish robar, ‘to steal’. And the same word, by way of rauba, gave French robe and so English robe. One trap for learners: la ropa is singular, though English ‘clothes’ is plural, so you say la ropa está limpia, not están.
historyEinfach: Ropa means ‘clothes’. The word is Germanic. It first meant things that people stole in war: goods and clothes. Later it meant cloth and clothes. The verb robar, ‘to steal’, is related to it. Remember: la ropa is singular in Spanish. We say la ropa está limpia, ‘the clothes are clean’.

elsewhere.text: French robe is the same word from the form rauba: for French speakers, clothes became one dress.
Portuguese roupa is the closest relative, with the same meaning.
